record.paper_title: Open Questions in Cosmic-Ray Research at Ultrahigh Energies
record.original_question: Why do extensive air-shower measurements at very high energies contain roughly 30-60% more muons than current hadronic-interaction models predict, and can the muon excess be explained by conventional improvements to Standard Model hadronic generators, or does it point to physics beyond the Standard Model?

evidence.quote: Depending on the interaction model used for reference and the measurement, there are about30−60% more muons found in data than predicted.

This muon puzzle is one of the most important problems in hadronic interaction physics as it is very difﬁcult, if not impossible, to increase the number of muons by such a large fraction just by changing the physics of the ﬁrst interaction.
First of all, there is the muon discrepancy that is still not understood.

Conventional explanations of the muon discrepancy have to be developed to ﬁnd out whether we indeed have to assume that the muon excess is related to physics beyond the Standard Model of particle physics.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Extensive air showers are cascades of secondary particles produced when an ultrahigh-energy cosmic ray (a primary nucleus or proton with laboratory energy above roughly 10^17 eV) interacts with nuclei in the Earth's atmosphere. The development of such a shower is simulated using hadronic-interaction generators (Monte Carlo models such as those tuned with accelerator data up to LHC energies) which predict, in particular, the number N_μ of muons reaching ground level as a function of primary energy E and primary mass A.

Multiple independent experiments measuring N_μ at primary energies E ≳ 10^17 eV consistently observe a muon content that exceeds the prediction of every contemporary hadronic-interaction model by approximately 30%–60%, depending on the experiment, the energy, and the reference model used. This systematic excess of measured ground-level muons over simulated muons is referred to as the muon puzzle.

Problem. Determine the physical origin of the muon excess in ultrahigh-energy extensive air showers. Specifically:

(a) Construct a quantitatively consistent modification of Standard Model hadronic interactions — for example, changes to the energy fraction carried by neutral pions, baryon-antibaryon pair production, strangeness enhancement, collective effects in pion–air or proton–air collisions, or other soft/forward QCD phenomena — that, when propagated through the full shower cascade, simultaneously reproduces the observed 30%–60% muon excess at ground level and remains consistent with all measured longitudinal shower observables (notably the depth of shower maximum X_max and its fluctuations) and with collider data on hadronic interactions.

(b) Decide whether such a Standard-Model-based modification is sufficient, or whether the observed muon excess necessarily requires a contribution from physics beyond the Standard Model.

A complete solution should specify the assumed hadronic-interaction modification (or new-physics mechanism), demonstrate via cascade simulation that the resulting N_μ matches measurements within experimental uncertainties across the relevant energy range, and verify compatibility with X_max measurements and accelerator constraints.
artifact.status_search_result: As of 2024–2025, the muon puzzle in ultrahigh-energy extensive air showers remains unresolved. Several candidate explanations have been proposed (collective/core-corona hadronization, gluon condensation, strangeness enhancement, and even Lorentz-invariance violation), but none has been confirmed as the definitive cause. New IceCube/IceTop measurements in 2025 continue to confirm and refine the discrepancy rather than resolve it, and the comprehensive 2022 review explicitly characterizes the puzzle as still open.

status_evidence.title: The Muon Puzzle in cosmic-ray induced air showers and its connection to the LHC
status_evidence.snippet: Comprehensive review identifying the muon excess in air showers as an unresolved problem connected to forward hadron production at the LHC.
status_evidence.claim: The muon puzzle is documented as an open problem in the most recent comprehensive review.

status_evidence.title: Improved IceTop measurements add to the cosmic-ray muon puzzle (IceCube, 2025)
status_evidence.snippet: New IceTop measurements in 2025 reinforce the existence of the muon discrepancy.
status_evidence.claim: Recent 2025 measurements continue to add to, rather than resolve, the muon puzzle.

status_evidence.title: Researchers find a possible solution to the cosmic ray muon puzzle (phys.org, 2024)
status_evidence.snippet: A 2024 paper proposes gluon condensation in the first cascade collision as a possible explanation, indicating the question is still actively being investigated.
status_evidence.claim: Candidate explanations are still being proposed in 2024, indicating the puzzle is not settled.
